items.stem: Which term describes a couple living together in a sexual relationship without being married or in a civil partnership?
items.answer: Cohabitation
items.markingKey: Cohabitation: a couple living together in a sexual relationship without being married or in a civil partnership. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “living apart together”, and give one example.
items.answer: A couple in a long-term relationship who choose to live in separate homes. Example: partners who each keep their own flat.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (a couple in a long-term relationship who choose to live in separate homes); 1 mark for a relevant example such as partners who each keep their own flat. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “cohabitation” and “serial monogamy”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Cohabitation: a couple living together in a sexual relationship without being married or in a civil partnership (e.g. a couple who have lived together for five years with no plans to marry). Serial monogamy: a pattern of having a series of marriages or long-term relationships, one after another (e.g. a person who marries, divorces and remarries twice).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Elena and her partner have lived together in Dhaka for eight years and have two children; they say marriage is “just a piece of paper”. Suggest how a New Right sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: New Right: the traditional nuclear family with married parents and a male breadwinner is the best environment for raising children; the growth of lone-parent families and cohabitation threatens social order and creates welfare dependency (Murray).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: In Jakarta, the average age at first marriage has risen from 23 to 31 over forty years. Explain how a radical feminist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Radical feminism: the family is a patriarchal institution in which men benefit from women’s unpaid domestic and emotional labour and domestic violence maintains male control (Delphy and Leonard).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A sociologist in Bogotá wants to research why couples choose to cohabit rather than marry. Evaluate the use of personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they show how people themselves understood their experiences; they may be the only source of evidence about the past. Limitations: their meaning must be interpreted by the researcher, which may introduce bias; they may not be authentic or credible; the writer may exaggerate or present themselves favourably. Theory: personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying why couples choose to cohabit rather than marry but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “arranged marriage”?
items.answer: A marriage in which families play a major role in choosing the partner.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: a marriage in which families play a major role in choosing the partner. [1]

items.stem: Grace and her partner have lived together in Madrid for eight years and have two children; they say marriage is “just a piece of paper”. Explain how New Right and radical feminist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: New Right: the traditional nuclear family with married parents and a male breadwinner is the best environment for raising children; the growth of lone-parent families and cohabitation threatens social order and creates welfare dependency (Murray). Radical feminism: the family is a patriarchal institution in which men benefit from women’s unpaid domestic and emotional labour and domestic violence maintains male control (Delphy and Leonard).

items.stem: Define the term “divorce”, and give one example.
items.answer: The legal ending of a marriage. Example: a court granting a decree ending a marriage.

items.stem: Distinguish between “stigma” and “no-fault divorce”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Stigma: a mark of disgrace or shame attached to a person or behaviour (e.g. divorced women being treated as outcasts in the past). No-fault divorce: divorce granted without either partner having to prove that the other was to blame (e.g. a divorce on the basis of irretrievable breakdown).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: After a new law in Hanoi allows couples to divorce without proving fault, the number of divorces doubles in two years. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: divorce reflects individual choice and the search for fulfilment; relationships are fluid and family types diverse (Stacey, Giddens).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Priya divorces her husband after 15 years, saying she was “tired of doing everything at home while working full-time”. Explain how a New Right sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: New Right: rising divorce is evidence of family breakdown, harming children and creating welfare dependency (Murray).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: After a new law in Mumbai allows couples to divorce without proving fault, the number of divorces doubles in two years. Explain how postmodernist and functionalist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Postmodernism: divorce reflects individual choice and the search for fulfilment; relationships are fluid and family types diverse (Stacey, Giddens). Functionalism: rising divorce reflects higher expectations of marriage; most people remarry, so marriage is still valued (Fletcher).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Assess how useful official statistics are for studying long-term trends in divorce.
items.answer: Strengths: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified; they are collected regularly, so trends over time and comparisons between groups can be made. Limitations: they are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs; they show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying long-term trends in divorce but best combined with another method such as personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using structured interviews to research long-term trends in divorce.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; every respondent is asked the same questions in the same order, so results are standardised and reliable. Limitations: the interviewer’s presence may produce interviewer bias or socially desirable answers; the fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying long-term trends in divorce but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). items.stem: Ethan, a single mother in Colombo, works part-time and struggles to pay rent; a newspaper column blames “broken families” for local crime. Suggest how a Marxist sociologist might explain this.

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) to research how same-sex couples organise family life.
items.answer: Strengths: they show how people themselves understood their experiences; they are often cheap to obtain and produced without the researcher influencing them. Limitations: they are usually unrepresentative because only some people keep or publish them; they may not be authentic or credible; the writer may exaggerate or present themselves favourably. Theory: personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how same-sex couples organise family life but best combined with another method such as official statistics (triangulation).

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) for studying relationships between step-parents and step-children.

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of self-completion questionnaires for studying changes in marriage rates since 1970.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; they are standardised, so the study can be repeated by another researcher to check reliability. items.stem: A sociologist in Cape Town wants to research children’s experiences of their parents’ divorce. Evaluate the use of structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: the interviewer can read questions aloud, so younger or less literate respondents can take part; the interviewer can explain unclear questions, so fewer answers are spoiled. Limitations: respondents may be reluctant to reveal sensitive information face to face to a stranger following a fixed script; the interviewer’s presence may produce interviewer bias or socially desirable answers. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying children’s experiences of their parents’ divorce but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes a family in which one or both partners have children from previous relationships?
items.answer: Reconstituted family
items.markingKey: Reconstituted family: a family in which one or both partners have children from previous relationships. [1]

items.stem: Explain two reasons for the increase in lone-parent families.
items.answer: Rising divorce and separation; declining stigma attached to births outside marriage; women’s economic independence; welfare support; some women choosing to have children alone.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained reason. [4]

items.stem: Ines, a single mother in Mumbai, works part-time and struggles to pay rent; a newspaper column blames “broken families” for local crime. Suggest how a New Right sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: New Right: the married, heterosexual two-parent family is the best environment for children; lone-parent and other non-traditional families are departures from this norm, and lone parenthood is linked to a lack of male role models and welfare dependency (Murray).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Tariq, a single mother in Muscat, works part-time and struggles to pay rent; a newspaper column blames “broken families” for local crime. Explain how a New Right sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: New Right: the married, heterosexual two-parent family is the best environment for children; lone-parent and other non-traditional families are departures from this norm, and lone parenthood is linked to a lack of male role models and welfare dependency (Murray).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Study the data, which come from a study of poverty among different family types (450 families with children, Toronto). Table: percentage of families in relative poverty | 2010 | 2025. Lone-parent families | 41% | 36%. Couple families with one earner | 30% | 32%. Couple families with two earners | 6% | 7%. (a) Suppose 150 of the respondents were Lone-parent families. Using the 2025 figure, calculate how many of them gave this response. (b) Explain one limitation of using official statistics to collect data like these. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that lone-parent families are a cause of poverty.
items.answer: (a) 36% of 150 = 36 ÷ 100 × 150 = 54 (to the nearest whole person). (b) Interpretivists argue they are social constructions shaped by the decisions of officials and the public. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Couple families with one earner, Couple families with two earners; the figure fell for Lone-parent families; Lone-parent families had the highest figure for 2025. Lone parents often cannot work full-time because of childcare, so incomes are lower. Qualifications: The data show a correlation, not causation: poverty may also cause relationship breakdown; policy (childcare, benefits) affects poverty; many lone-parent families are not poor. The data also come from official statistics of 450 families with children in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark method (36 ÷ 100 × 150); 1 mark answer 54. [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: State one reason why family size has fallen in many societies.
items.answer: Contraception is widely available.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. contraception is widely available. [1]

items.stem: Explain two reasons why the birth rate has fallen in many societies.
items.answer: Women’s greater participation in education and paid work; availability of contraception and abortion; falling infant mortality; children are an economic cost rather than an asset; changing attitudes and later marriage.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained reason. [4]

items.stem: Sipho, a sociology student, is designing a project on why couples decide how many children to have. Evaluate the use of participant observation for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: it reveals the meanings and labels that shape interaction as it happens; by joining the group the researcher can gain verstehen and see the world through members’ eyes. Limitations: it is very difficult to observe private behaviour inside homes; the observer’s presence may change the group’s behaviour (the Hawthorne effect), especially if overt. Theory: participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying why couples decide how many children to have but best combined with another method such as structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]
